Cic. Cael. 59: saepe mē, saepissimē rem pūblicam
Traupman 353

saepe

adverb; comparative saepius, superlative saepissimē · Wiktionary

The everyday word, of things that happen again and again at intervals; Lewis & Short contrasts crēbrō, of things that come close one after another. How often? is quotiēns? (Traupman 87; see whenever).

Other words

  • crēbrō — often, repeatedly, again and again

    adverb · also used · classical · Cic. Att. 7.10.1: crēbrō ad mē scrībe; Cato Agr. 48.2: crēbrō runcātō · Wiktionary

    Of things that come thick and fast (Lewis & Short): letters, coughing, hoeing. The adjective crēber is first thick, close-set (trees, buildings), then frequent.

  • frequenter — frequently, often

    adverb · also used · classical · Quint. 1.8.11 (Lewis & Short); Petr. 66.1 · Wiktionary

    Not common until after Augustus (Lewis & Short): Quintilian uses it often, and so do Petronius’s freedmen. It also means in great numbers (Liv. 1.11.4). The adjective frequēns is first of people often in a place or often doing a thing (frequēns audītor, a regular hearer), then of things that happen often.

  • saepenumerō — very often, many a time

    adverb · also used · classical · Lewis & Short, s.v. saepe · Wiktionary

Examples

  • crēbrō Catulum, saepe mē, saepissimē rem pūblicam nōminābat

    he kept naming Catulus, often me, and most often of all the RepublicCic. Cael. 59

  • tū, quaesō, crēbrō ad mē scrībe vel quod in buccam vēnerit

    please write to me often, even just whatever comes into your headCic. Att. 7.10.1

  • crēbrō runcātō. simul herbae incēperint nāscī, eximitō

    weed often; as soon as the weeds start coming up, pull them outCato Agr. 48.2

  • nam tam bonae memoriae sum, ut frequenter nōmen meum oblīvīscar

    for my memory is so good that I often forget my own namePetr. 66.1

See also sometimes, always, every so often, whenever, never.
